title: God is love (1 John 4:7–12)
hook: whoever loves is born of God, for God is love
carry: love, and do what you will

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word discernment, and your line was test the spirits. Which claim did you check before you shared it? Day six hundred eighty-nine.

Church signs. Wedding programs. Bumper stickers. A pillow stitched in a grandmother's living room. The same three words turn up on all of them, printed so often they can start to sound like wallpaper. But they began in this letter, and they were not written as decoration. The writer has just told his readers to test every spirit, to watch out for voices that sound right and aren't. And then, right after that warning, he sets down the line all those signs borrowed. Today we hear those three words where they actually live.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God." Love comes from God, the way light comes from the sun. Then the reverse: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." Notice the order of those words. God is love. Not love is God. In the Greek the grammar makes that clear: God is the subject. The writer isn't saying that whatever we feel as love is divine. He's saying something about who God is: love belongs to God's very nature. So how do we know what that love looks like? He doesn't leave it abstract. "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." The love starts on God's side, not ours. Propitiation is a heavy word; it means the offering that makes things right between us and God. Christians explain how that works in different ways, but they agree on the direction: love reaching first. Then a startling line: "No man hath seen God at any time." Nobody. And yet, the next words: "If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us." In the writer's telling, the unseen God is found, in a sense, wherever people love. Centuries later, Augustine preached a series of sermons on this letter. In one of them he said, in Latin, dilige, et quod vis fac: love, and do what you will. He didn't mean anything goes. He meant that if love is the root within, what grows from it will be good.
screen: `GOD IS LOVE, NOT LOVE IS GOD.`
`HE LOVED US FIRST, AND SENT HIS SON.`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD. LOVE SHOWS HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone without conditions, starting here. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you love, but with a few conditions attached. If they'd only call more. If they'd stop that habit. If they'd say sorry first. Picture their face. Then, gently, set the conditions down, one at a time, as if you were taking stones out of your pockets. What's left when they're gone? Stay with that. Notice how it feels to love them as they are, this minute. If you pray, you can hold their name before God, just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Agape. Greek for self-giving love: First John's claim that God is love, not that love is God, and that love belongs to God's very nature.
Your line: love, and do what you will. Today, with the person you pictured, drop one condition for one whole day, and see what changes. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: 1 John 4:7–12 is read at some Christian weddings and funerals, and some churches teach children 'God is love' as a first, short summary of the faith.

fork.setup: nobody has ever seen God, the letter admits. so where, according to the writer, can God's love be seen?
fork.reveal: "If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us."

original.note: Greek: love, especially self-giving love. the word in ho theos agapē estin, God is love.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice sentiment on a pillow.
what it means: the letter names God as love, a love that reached us first and that, the writer says, dwells in people who love one another.
what a scholar hears: ho theos agapē estin, with God as the grammatical subject, so it can't be flipped to 'love is God'; and Augustine's sermons on this letter, with dilige, et quod vis fac.
recall: lights in the sky, as in Genesis

notes: Augustine, Tractates/Homilies on 1 John 7.8: 'Dilige, et quod vis fac.' The translation 'love, and do what you will' is the script's own. Confirm reference. ('Four centuries later' was cut to 'centuries later' in review.)
Greek grammar of 4:8 (ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν; article marks θεός as subject): standard. Confirm.
Propitiation (ἱλασμός): glossed simply; Christians differ on atonement theories, acknowledged in one line. Confirm.
